pamphlet_excerpts: Overhead Catenary Pantograph Collection: Electric locomotives (without a diesel engine) collect current from overhead wires, orcatenary, through metal arms called pantographs mounted (p. 15).
Electrified Third Rail Pickups: Others use a pickup shoe to collect current from an electrified third rail placed next to the running rails (p. 15).
Internal Voltage Conversion Equipment: The locomotive's internal equipment converts high-voltage current to lower voltage current (p. 15).
Push and Pull Commuter Configurations: Locomotives, especially on passenger commuter trains, often push as well as pull their trains (p. 15).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Convert High Voltage Current: The locomotive's internal equipment converts high-voltage current to lower voltage current (p. 15).
Step 2 - Push and Pull Trains: Locomotives, especially on passenger commuter trains, often push as well as pull their trains (p. 15).
Step 3 - Operate Duplicate Cab Controls: The train has a locomotive on one end and a passenger car equipped with an engineer's cab and duplicate controls on the other end (p. 15).
Step 4 - Apply Train Air Brakes: A train stops by using an air brake system, which allows the engineer to apply the brakes to all cars at once (p. 15).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Why does Operation Lifesaver emphasize that pedestrians and drivers must never walk along railroad tracks or drive around lowered crossing gates?
quiz_item.question: Why does Operation Lifesaver emphasize that pedestrians and drivers must never walk along railroad tracks or drive around lowered crossing gates?
options: A. Trains can easily swerve onto adjacent tracks, making it hard to predict which rail they will use.
B. A freight train overhangs the rails by at least three feet on both sides, can approach quietly, and often requires more than a mile to stop even with emergency braking.
C. Railroad tracks carry high-voltage third-rail traction power on all rural diesel freight lines across North America.
D. Crossing gates lower only after the locomotive is within 50 feet of the intersection.
choices: A. Trains can easily swerve onto adjacent tracks, making it hard to predict which rail they will use.
B. A freight train overhangs the rails by at least three feet on both sides, can approach quietly, and often requires more than a mile to stop even with emergency braking.
C. Railroad tracks carry high-voltage third-rail traction power on all rural diesel freight lines across North America.
D. Crossing gates lower only after the locomotive is within 50 feet of the intersection.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. A freight train overhangs the rails by at least three feet on both sides, can approach quietly, and often requires more than a mile to stop even with emergency braking.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Trains cannot steer, overhang the crossties, appear slower and farther away than they actually are, and require a mile or more to come to a full stop.

pamphlet_excerpts: Host Freight Railroad Track age: Today Amtrak carries more than 31 million passengers ayear over more than 22,000 miles of track, almost all of it owned by the Class I freight railroads (p. 27).
Northeast Corridor Electrified Line: The exception is the Northeast Corridor (NEC), where Amtrak owns and maintains most of this high-speed electrified rail line between Boston (p. 27).
High Speed Corridor Expansion: Long-term plans are under way to extend this rail corridor south to Richmond, Virginia, and add other high-speed lines in California, the upper (p. 27).
Michigan Line Track Ownership: It also owns a 97-mile segment between Porter, Indiana, and Kalamazoo, Michigan (p. 27).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Plan High Speed Corridors: Long-term plans are under way to extend this rail corridor south to Richmond, Virginia, and add other high-speed lines in California, the upper (p. 27).
Step 2 - Maintain Dedicated Michigan Track age: It also owns a 97-mile segment between Porter, Indiana, and Kalamazoo, Michigan (p. 27).
Step 3 - Deploy Cleaner Siemens Locomotives: On long-distance routes, Amtrak is replacing older diesel locomotives with fuel efficient and cleaner-burning ALC-42 locomotives from Siemens (p. 27).
Step 4 - Reduce Diesel Exhaust Emissions: These engines emit 89% less nitrogen oxide and 95% less particulate matter than the old diesels (p. 27).

requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following special-interest options: (a) Option A, Model Railroading. With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, do TWO of the following: (1) Draw a layout of your own model railroad or one that could be built in your home. Design a point-to-point track or loop with different routings. Include one of the following: turnaround or terminal or yard or siding. (2) Build one model railroad car kit or one locomotive kit. (3) Name the scale of four popular model railroad gauges. Identify the scale of four model cars or locomotives. (4) Locate the websites of four model railroad-related manufacturers or magazine publishers. Print information about their products and services, and discuss the information with your counselor. (5) Build one railroad structure (from scratch or using a kit), paint and weather the structure, mount it on your layout or diorama, and make the surrounding area on the diorama scenic. (6) Alone or with others, build a model railroad or modular layout including ballast and scenery. Make electrical connections and operate a train. Describe what you enjoyed most. (7) Participate in a switching contest on a timesaver layout and record your time. (8) Explain the difference between powering and controlling a model railroad by using direct current, and powering and controlling a model railroad using digital command control. (b) Option B, Railfanning. With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, do TWO of the following: (1) Visit a railroad museum, historical display, or a prototype railroad-sponsored public event. With permission, photograph, digitally record, or sketch items of interest. Explain what you saw and describe your photos, sketches, or video. (2) Purchase tickets and ride a scenic or historic railroad. Under supervision, photograph the equipment and discuss with your counselor the historic significance of the operation. (3) Locate the websites of four rail historical groups, then find information on the history of the rail preservation operations and purpose of each group. Talk with a member of one of the groups and find out how you might help. (4) Plan a trip by rail between two points. Obtain a schedule and explain when the train should arrive at two intermediate points. Purchase the tickets and make the trip. Explain to your counselor what you saw.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option A, Model Railroading. With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, do TWO of the following: (1) Draw a layout of your own model railroad or one that could be built in your home. Design a point-to-point track or loop with different routings. Include one of the following: turnaround or terminal or yard or siding. (2) Build one model railroad car kit or one locomotive kit. (3) Name the scale of four popular model railroad gauges. Identify the scale of four model cars or locomotives. (4) Locate the websites of four model railroad-related manufacturers or magazine publishers. Print information about their products and services, and discuss the information with your counselor. (5) Build one railroad structure (from scratch or using a kit), paint and weather the structure, mount it on your layout or diorama, and make the surrounding area on the diorama scenic. (6) Alone or with others, build a model railroad or modular layout including ballast and scenery. Make electrical connections and operate a train. Describe what you enjoyed most. (7) Participate in a switching contest on a timesaver layout and record your time. (8) Explain the difference between powering and controlling a model railroad by using direct current, and powering and controlling a model railroad using digital command control.

sub_requirements.label: (b)
sub_requirements.text: Option B, Railfanning. With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, do TWO of the following: (1) Visit a railroad museum, historical display, or a prototype railroad-sponsored public event. With permission, photograph, digitally record, or sketch items of interest. Explain what you saw and describe your photos, sketches, or video. (2) Purchase tickets and ride a scenic or historic railroad. Under supervision, photograph the equipment and discuss with your counselor the historic significance of the operation. (3) Locate the websites of four rail historical groups, then find information on the history of the rail preservation operations and purpose of each group. Talk with a member of one of the groups and find out how you might help. (4) Plan a trip by rail between two points. Obtain a schedule and explain when the train should arrive at two intermediate points. Purchase the tickets and make the trip. Explain to your counselor what you saw.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Why does Operation Lifesaver emphasize that pedestrians and drivers must never walk along railroad tracks or drive around lowered crossing gates?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why does Operation Lifesaver emphasize that pedestrians and drivers must never walk along railroad tracks or drive around lowered crossing gates?
options: A. Trains can easily swerve onto adjacent tracks, making it hard to predict which rail they will use.
B. A freight train overhangs the rails by at least three feet on both sides, can approach quietly, and often requires more than a mile to stop even with emergency braking.
C. Railroad tracks carry high-voltage third-rail traction power on all rural diesel freight lines across North America.
D. Crossing gates lower only after the locomotive is within 50 feet of the intersection.
choices: A. Trains can easily swerve onto adjacent tracks, making it hard to predict which rail they will use.
B. A freight train overhangs the rails by at least three feet on both sides, can approach quietly, and often requires more than a mile to stop even with emergency braking.
C. Railroad tracks carry high-voltage third-rail traction power on all rural diesel freight lines across North America.
D. Crossing gates lower only after the locomotive is within 50 feet of the intersection.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. A freight train overhangs the rails by at least three feet on both sides, can approach quietly, and often requires more than a mile to stop even with emergency braking.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Trains cannot steer, overhang the crossties, appear slower and farther away than they actually are, and require a mile or more to come to a full stop.

choices: A. The transportation department

options: A. Platform edges are electrified with high-voltage current
B. Station platforms sink several inches under train weight
C. The locomotive engineer cannot see passengers on platforms
D. Trains overhang the tracks and are wider than the rails
choices: A. Platform edges are electrified with high-voltage current

patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Trains are wider than the tracks and overhang the rails on both sides, so passengers must always stand behind the safety line and never sit on the platform edge (p. 38).

B. Avoid the crossing because low-clearance vehicles risk getting hung up on the tracks
C. Lower the trailer's tire pressure to increase traction on the steel rails
D. Stop on the tracks and call the railroad dispatcher for a pilot car
